title_en: Pulanna Life Art Co., Ltd. v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce — administrative dispute over rejection of trademark application and review
ruling_gist_en: When an applicant claims priority rights during trademark registration, and the administrative department fails to examine whether the applied-for trademark enjoys priority rights, resulting in an erroneous decision under review, the people's court shall, after ascertaining the relevant facts, render a judgment in accordance with the law.
keywords_en: Administrative; Administrative dispute over review of trademark application refusal; Retrial; Supreme People's Court; Beijing; Legal person; State organ; Trademark Law; Determination of priority right; Judgment on trademark similarity; Judgment on similarity of goods; Reversal of judgment; Trademark registration application; Claim of priority right; Review of trademark refusal; Application for retrial; Trademark registration
full_text_en:
PRANA LIVING, LLC v.

Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce — administrative dispute over trademark application rejection review

【Ruling Summary】

Where an applicant claims priority at the time of filing a trademark registration application, and the administrative authority, in reviewing whether the applied-for trademark is entitled to priority, commits an omission that results in an erroneous decision under review, the people's court shall render a judgment based on the facts ascertained and in accordance with the law.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Judgment

(2017) Zui Gao Fa Xing Zai No. 10

Re-Petitioner (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): PRANA LIVING, LLC. Address: 3209 Lion's Head Street, Carlsbad, California, United States of America.

Legal Representative: Adam R. Kelly, Assistant Secretary of the company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Zheng, attorney at Beijing Dongquan Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Deng Tianmei, attorney at Beijing Dongquan Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce. Address: No. 1, Chama Nan Jie, Xicheng District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Zhao Gang, Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Jia Qiushi, Examiner of the Board.

The re-petitioner, PRANA LIVING, LLC (hereinafter referred to as PRANA), filed a petition for retrial with this court, dissatisfied with the administrative judgment (2015) Gao Xing (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 3778 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court in the case of the administrative dispute over trademark application rejection review against the respondent, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Review Board). On December 28, 2016, this court issued the administrative ruling (2016) Zui Gao Fa Xing Shen No. 2221, granting the retrial and taking jurisdiction over the case. After the retrial was granted, this lawfully formed a collegial panel and conducted a hearing. The hearing has now been concluded.

PRANA alleged in its petition for retrial: (1) The priority date of the applied-for trademark is earlier than the filing date of the first cited trademark, and the applied-for trademark designated for use on "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" should be approved for registration. The priority certificate and trademark records submitted by PRANA prove that the priority date of the applied-for trademark is November 19, 2010, which is earlier than the filing date of the first cited trademark, November 26, 2010. The Trademark Review Board's finding that the first cited trademark was a prior trademark was a factual error. The decision under review, Shang Biao Ping Zi [2013] No. 129449 regarding the rejection review of trademark registration application No. 8996648 "prAna and design" (hereinafter referred to as the Decision under Review), as well as the judgments of the first and second instances, were insufficiently supported by evidence regarding material facts. (2) The findings in the Decision under Review and the judgments of the first and second instances that the goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" designated for use by the applied-for trademark and the goods "skateboards" approved for use by the first cited trademark were similar goods, and that the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark were similar, were insufficiently supported by evidence, leading to erroneous application of the law. 1. The goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" designated for use by the applied-for trademark are not similar goods to the "skateboards" approved for use by the first cited trademark. 2. There are certain differences in overall appearance and composition between the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark. Use of the applied-for trademark on "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" and the first cited trademark on "skateboards" would not cause confusion or misidentification. 3. Used on their respective designated/approved goods, the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark are sufficient to serve as indicators of the origin of the goods. 4. PRANA has used the applied-for trademark extensively in advertising and marketing promotions. The applied-for trademark has established a close or even exclusive association with PRANA, sufficient to distinguish it from the first cited trademark. Registration and use of the applied-for trademark would not cause confusion or misidentification among the relevant public and should be permitted. In summary, PRANA requested that the judgments of the first and second instances and the Decision under Review be quashed, and that the respondent be ordered to issue a new decision.

The Trademark Review Board argued in its defense: (1) The goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" designated for use by the applied-for trademark and the goods "skateboards" approved for use by the first cited trademark are closely related in terms of consumer targets and sales channels, and thus are similar goods. The applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark constitute similar trademarks used on identical or similar goods. (2) Although it has been verified that PRANA had submitted documents claiming priority, the Trademark Office nevertheless treated the first cited trademark as the cited trademark in this case during examination, demonstrating that the priority of the applied-for trademark was not recognized. In summary, the Trademark Review Board requested that the judgments of the first and second instances and the Decision under Review be upheld.

During the retrial petition stage, PRANA submitted the trademark records of the applied-for trademark and the application materials for the applied-for trademark. The trademark registration application form bore the official seal of Beijing East IP Co., Ltd., which recorded that the country of first priority application was the United States and the application date was November 19, 2010. In a "Statement on Priority Documents" addressed to the Trademark Office, Beijing East IP Co., Ltd. stated that PRANA filed an application for registration of the applied-for trademark on goods in Class 28 on December 28, 2010, which also recorded the country of first priority application, the application date, and the application number. Meanwhile, PRANA submitted materials showing that it had filed a priority claim within the statutory period, and the Archives Department of the Trademark Office stamped and acknowledged the authenticity of those materials.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found upon trial that on December 28, 2010, PRANA filed an application with the Trademark Office for registration of trademark No. 8996648 "prAna and design," designating use on goods in International Class 28, groups 2807 and 2809: "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps; climbing belts."

The first cited trademark was trademark No. 8885559 "Prana," with a filing date of November 26, 2010, owned by Blue Hat (Xiamen) Cultural Communication Co., Ltd., with a trademark term from October 14, 2012 to October 13, 2022. The approved goods were in International Class 28, groups 2801-2804, 2807, and 2810: "video game machines; electric amusement vehicles; toys; toy cars; intelligent toys; children's scooters (toys); chess; sports balls; skateboards; Christmas tree decorations (except lighting articles and confectionery)." Only "skateboards" fell within group 2807.

The second cited trademark was trademark No. G686680 "PRADA and design," with an international registration date of December 23, 1997, owned by Prada S.A., with a right term from December 23, 2007 to December 23, 2017. The approved goods were in International Class 28, groups 2801-2807, 2809-2811: "entertainment articles; toys; sporting and athletic goods not included in other classes; Christmas tree decorations."

On March 27, 2012, the Trademark Office issued the "Notice of Trademark Rejection," finding that the applied-for trademark was similar to the first and second cited trademarks and rejected the registration application of the applied-for trademark. PRANA disagreed and applied for review to the Trademark Review Board on April 16, 2012, requesting approval of the registration application of the applied-for trademark. The main reasons were: the applied-for trademark was not similar to the cited trademarks; the applicant and the owner of the second cited trademark were negotiating a coexistence agreement; the applied-for trademark had strong distinctiveness and, through extensive promotion and use by the applicant, had gained considerable reputation in the industry and was well-known to the relevant public, and would not cause confusion or misidentification among consumers.

On December 9, 2013, the Trademark Review Board issued the Decision under Review, holding that the words "prAna" of the applied-for trademark, the words "Prana" of the first cited trademark No. 8885559, and the words "PRADA" of the second cited trademark No. G686680 were all composed of multiple English letters, similar in letter composition and pronunciation, with only minor differences in individual letters. Consumers exercising ordinary attention under isolated conditions would find it difficult to distinguish them, and they constituted similar marks. The goods "yoga bricks, yoga boards, yoga straps, climbing belts" designated for use by the applied-for trademark and the goods "skateboards" etc. approved for use by the first cited trademark were similar in function, purpose, sales venues, etc., and were identical or similar goods. The coexistence of the applied-for trademark with the first and second cited trademarks on the above goods would easily lead the relevant public to confuse or misidentify the source of the goods. Therefore, the applied-for trademark and the first and second cited trademarks constituted similar trademarks used on identical or similar goods. The evidence provided by PRANA was insufficient to prove that the applied-for trademark, through use, had gained considerable recognition sufficient to distinguish it from the first and second cited trademarks. Pursuant to Article 28 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2001) (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law), the applied-for trademark was rejected.

PRANA, dissatisfied with the Decision under Review, filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, alleging that the applied-for trademark was not similar to the first and second cited trademarks; PRANA enjoyed legally protected enterprise name rights to the applied-for trademark, and its registration had a reasonable and lawful basis and should be approved; through extensive publicity and use, the applied-for trademark enjoyed considerable recognition and complied with the Trademark Law and other relevant laws regarding trademark registration. PRANA requested that the Decision under Review be quashed and the Trademark Review Board be ordered to issue a new decision.

The Trademark Review Board argued that the Decision under Review was based on clear facts, correctly applied the law, and was made in accordance with lawful procedures, and requested that the court uphold the Decision under Review and order PRANA to bear the litigation costs.

During the first-instance trial, PRANA produced a notarized and authenticated letter of consent (original) from Prada S.A., the owner of the second cited trademark. In the letter, Prada S.A. consented to the registration of the applied-for trademark in China for goods in Class 28: "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps; climbing belts."

The first-instance court held, first, regarding whether the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark constituted similar trademarks on similar goods. The goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" designated for use by the applied-for trademark and the goods "skateboards" approved for use by the first cited trademark both fell within group 2807 "gymnastics, weightlifting, track and field, ice and snow, and other sports equipment belonging to this class" and constituted similar goods. The goods "climbing belts" designated for use by the applied-for trademark and the goods "skateboards" etc. approved for use by the first cited trademark did not constitute similar goods. The English word portion "prAna" of the applied-for trademark and the English word "Prana" of the first cited trademark were not significantly different, had the same pronunciation, and constituted similar signs. The applied-for trademark designated for use on "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" and the first cited trademark already constituted similar trademarks on similar goods. PRANA's claim that the applied-for trademark, through long-term publicity and use, had gained considerable recognition sufficient to avoid confusion or misidentification lacked factual and legal basis and was not supported. Second, regarding whether the applied-for trademark and the second cited trademark constituted similar trademarks on similar goods. The evidence on file showed that Prada S.A., the owner of the second cited trademark, had issued a letter of consent agreeing to the registration of the applied-for trademark in China for goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps; climbing belts." Considering this situation and the fact that the applied-for trademark and the second cited trademark were not completely identical in form, the second cited trademark was no longer a prior rights obstacle to the registration of the applied-for trademark on all goods. Additionally, PRANA's claim that it enjoyed legally protected enterprise name rights to the applied-for trademark and that the applied-for trademark should therefore be approved for registration lacked legal basis and was not supported. In summary, pursuant to Article 54, Paragraph (2), Items 1 and 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (1989), the court quashed the Decision under Review and ordered the Trademark Review Board to issue a new decision on PRANA's application for review of the rejection.

PRANA, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, arguing that the goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" designated for use by the applied-for trademark and the goods "skateboards" approved for use by the first cited trademark were not similar in function, purpose, sales channels, consumer groups, etc.; the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark did not constitute similar trademarks; use of the applied-for trademark on "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" and the first cited trademark on "skateboards" would not cause confusion or misidentification. PRANA requested that the portion of the first-instance judgment that refused to approve registration of the applied-for trademark designated for use on "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" be quashed and amended accordingly.

The second-instance court held upon trial that the goods "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" designated for use by the applied-for trademark, though not standard goods in the Classification of Similar Goods and Services, were closely related to the goods "skateboards" approved for use by the first cited trademark in terms of production departments, consumer targets, and sales channels, with substantial overlap, making it easy for the relevant public to believe that the goods were provided by the same entity or that there was a specific relationship between the providers, thus constituting similar goods. The distinctive part of the applied-for trademark was completely identical to the first cited trademark in English letter composition, arrangement, and pronunciation. Although there were minor differences in font and overall design, these could not achieve a significant distinguishing effect. If the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark were used together on similar goods, it would easily cause confusion and misidentification among the relevant public regarding the source of the goods, and they constituted similar trademarks. The evidence provided by PRANA during the first-instance proceedings was insufficient to prove that the applied-for trademark, before the filing date of the first cited trademark, had gained considerable recognition in China through use sufficient to distinguish it from the first cited trademark. Trademark review cases follow the principle of individual case examination. The other trademark registration situations cited by PRANA differed from the facts of this case and could not serve as automatic grounds for the registration of the applied-for trademark. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed and the original judgment was affirmed.

Regarding the retrial requests of the parties, this court ascertained the following facts:

PRANA, based on its application for the "prAna and design" trademark filed in the United States on November 19, 2010, filed a registration application for the applied-for trademark with the Trademark Office on December 28, 2010, claiming priority in the application form, and submitted the corresponding priority certificate on January 27, 2011. The priority date of the applied-for trademark is November 19, 2010.

After the Beijing High People's Court rendered the administrative judgment (2015) Gao Xing (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 3778, the Trademark Review Board issued on January 27, 2016 the "Decision on Rejection Review of Trademark Registration Application No. 8996648 'prAna and design'," concluding that the registration application of the applied-for trademark designated for use on "climbing belts" was to be preliminarily approved, and the registration applications designated for use on the remaining goods under review were to be rejected. On March 29, 2016, PRANA, dissatisfied with this decision, filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing Intellectual Property Court, arguing that it did not object to the preliminary approval of the registration application for "climbing belts," but that the portion rejecting the registration application for "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps" was based on erroneous factual findings and should be quashed. One of the reasons was that the Trademark Review Board's finding that the first cited trademark was a prior trademark was a factual error; the priority date of the applied-for trademark was earlier than the filing date of the first cited trademark, so the applied-for trademark should be considered the prior trademark.

This court holds that the focal issue in this case is whether, with respect to the applied-for trademark designated for use on "yoga bricks; yoga boards; yoga straps," the first cited trademark constitutes an obstacle to the rights for its registration.

Article 24 of the Trademark Law provides: "If a trademark registration applicant, within six months from the date on which it first filed an application for registration of the trademark in a foreign country, files an application for registration of the same trademark on the same goods in China, it may, in accordance with any agreement concluded between that foreign country and China or any international treaty to which both are parties, or according to the principle of mutual recognition of priority, enjoy the right of priority." "Any person who claims the right of priority in accordance with the preceding paragraph shall, when filing the application for trademark registration, make a written statement and, within three months, submit the copy of the first application for trademark registration; if no written statement is made or the copy of the application for trademark registration is not submitted within the time limit, the claim for the right of priority shall be deemed not to have been made." This article provides for the acquisition and procedure of priority in China for trademarks already applied for abroad. In this case, the filing date of the first cited trademark is November 26, 2010. According to the facts ascertained, the priority date of the applied-for trademark is November 19, 2010. The priority date of the applied-for trademark is earlier than the filing date of the first cited trademark.

PRANA had previously claimed priority during the administrative procedures for trademark authorization. The Trademark Office did not respond to that claim, and the Trademark Review Board failed to recognize this fact during the review stage, resulting in the Decision under Review omitting a matter that the party had raised. The courts of first and second instances both ordered the Trademark Review Board to issue a new decision on the applied-for trademark, but the basic fact regarding the determination of priority was not addressed in the new decision issued by the Trademark Review Board. Because the determination of priority is key to determining whether the first cited trademark constitutes an obstacle to the rights for the applied-for trademark, and PRANA again filed an administrative lawsuit against the new trademark rejection review decision, given that the Decision under Review omitted the priority date of the applied-for trademark, leading to the erroneous conclusion that the first cited trademark was an obstacle to registration, to avoid circular litigation, protect the rights and interests of the parties in a timely manner, and improve judicial efficiency, this court, by reference to Article 2 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation, "The scope of review by the people's court of administrative acts concerning trademark authorization and confirmation shall generally be determined based on the plaintiff's claims and reasons. Where the plaintiff has not raised a claim in the lawsuit, but the relevant finding of the Trademark Review Board is clearly improper, the people's court may, after hearing the opinions of the parties, examine the relevant matter and render a judgment," hereby corrects the erroneous finding in the Decision under Review, namely, that the priority date of the applied-for trademark is November 19, 2010, not December 28, 2010. Because the priority date of the applied-for trademark is earlier than the filing date of the first cited trademark, the first cited trademark does not constitute an obstacle to the rights for the registration of the applied-for trademark. Under such circumstances, there is no need to discuss whether the applied-for trademark and the first cited trademark constitute similar trademarks on identical or similar goods.

In summary, the grounds for Pulanna Company's retrial application regarding the priority right are well-founded. The appealed decision made by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board was erroneous in its conclusion and should be revoked. The judgments of the first and second instance, which upheld the erroneous determination of the appealed decision, should also be revoked. Pursuant to Article 24 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (revised in 2001), Article 70 and Article 89, Paragraph 1(2) and Paragraph 3 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (revised in 2014), and Article 76, Paragraph 1 and Article 78 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. The Administrative Judgment (2015) Gao Xing (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 3778 of the Beijing High People's Court is hereby revoked;

2. The Administrative Judgment (2014) Yi Zhong Xing (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 7996 of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court is hereby revoked;

3. The Decision Shang Ping Zi [2013] No. 129449 of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce regarding the review of refusal of trademark No. 8996648 "prAna and design" is hereby revoked;

4. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce shall make a new decision on the review of refusal of trademark No. 8996648 "prAna and design".

The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 and the second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board.

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Zhou Xiang

Acting Judge: Luo Xia

Acting Judge: Tong Shu

May 9, 2017
